title: Industrial Warehouse Discovery
name: Industrial Warehouse Discovery
metaTitle: Industrial Warehouse Discovery in Los Angeles, CA
metaDescription: Identifying modern distribution facilities and flex space in the Inland Empire and greater Los Angeles logistics corridors for 1031 exchange replacement.

sections.html: The Inland Empire and broader Los Angeles basin remain among the tightest industrial logistics markets in the country, which makes discovering an available warehouse or distribution facility within a forty five day identification window genuinely difficult without an active, pre-built pipeline of relationships and off-market leads.

sections.heading: Clear Height and Functional Specifications Drive Value
sections.html: Modern logistics tenants generally require clear ceiling heights of thirty two feet or more, ample trailer parking, and sufficient dock door ratios, and older Los Angeles industrial stock built to lower clear heights functions differently in the leasing market than newer big-box product in the Inland Empire. We evaluate a candidate building's functional specifications against current tenant demand rather than relying on age or location alone.

sections.heading: Single Tenant Versus Multi-Tenant Flex Buildings
sections.html: A single-tenant distribution facility on a long-term corporate lease behaves more like a NNN investment, while a multi-tenant flex building with smaller bay sizes carries more active leasing and management responsibility but can offer diversified rent roll exposure. We help exchangers weigh this tradeoff against how much ongoing management involvement they want after closing.

sections.heading: Environmental Due Diligence on Industrial Property
sections.html: Prior industrial use raises the likelihood of environmental considerations, from historical fuel storage to soil contamination, that require a Phase I environmental site assessment before closing, and we flag this diligence need early in the identification process so it does not become a bottleneck against the one hundred eighty day closing deadline.

sections.heading: Expanding the Search Beyond the Immediate Los Angeles Basin
sections.html: Because available industrial inventory in the core Los Angeles basin is limited and expensive, we generally expand the search into the Inland Empire logistics corridors along the Interstate 10 and Interstate 15 corridors, where newer big-box product is more readily available and often better suited to current tenant demand.

sections.heading: Power Capacity as an Increasingly Important Specification
sections.html: Beyond clear height and dock ratios, available electrical power capacity has become an increasingly important specification for logistics and light manufacturing tenants in the Los Angeles basin, and older industrial buildings sometimes carry legacy power infrastructure that is expensive to upgrade; we ask about power capacity and any recent upgrades as part of evaluating a candidate building's functional fit.

sections.heading: Truck Court Depth and Circulation for Modern Logistics Use
sections.html: Beyond clear height, adequate truck court depth and efficient circulation for trailer maneuvering have become important criteria for logistics tenants, and older Los Angeles basin industrial buildings on tighter sites sometimes cannot accommodate the truck court depth modern distribution use requires, which affects which tenant profile a given building can realistically attract.

faqs.q: What clear height do modern logistics tenants typically require?
faqs.a: Generally thirty two feet or more for large distribution users, though smaller flex or last-mile facilities can function well with lower clear heights depending on the tenant profile targeted.

faqs.q: Does older industrial stock in Los Angeles still attract strong tenant demand?
faqs.a: It can, particularly for last-mile and infill logistics uses close to population centers, though older buildings with lower clear heights are generally less suited to large-scale distribution tenants than newer Inland Empire product.

faqs.q: Is a Phase I environmental site assessment always required on industrial property?
faqs.a: It is standard practice given the history of fuel storage, chemical use, and similar activity common on industrial sites, and most lenders require it before financing an industrial acquisition regardless of the specific property's known history.

faqs.q: Why would an exchanger consider the Inland Empire instead of Los Angeles County itself?
faqs.a: Available inventory is generally greater and pricing more accessible in the Inland Empire logistics corridors, and much of that product is newer construction built to current tenant specifications.

faqs.q: How does a single-tenant industrial lease compare to a multi-tenant flex building for a passive investor?
faqs.a: A single-tenant lease on a long-term corporate guarantee generally requires less active management, similar to a NNN retail investment, while a multi-tenant flex building involves more ongoing leasing activity but can diversify income across several tenants.

faqs.q: Does electrical power capacity matter for industrial tenant demand?
faqs.a: Increasingly yes; available power capacity has become an important specification for logistics and light manufacturing tenants, and older buildings with legacy infrastructure can be expensive to upgrade.

faqs.q: Does truck court depth matter as much as clear height for industrial tenants?
faqs.a: It matters considerably for logistics and distribution tenants specifically, since adequate depth and circulation for trailer maneuvering is often a hard requirement, and older buildings on tighter sites sometimes cannot meet it regardless of otherwise adequate clear height.
